chunks: What brushes are made of. The question: What are brushes made out of?
Most motor brushes are made of carbon, usually a carbon-graphite mix.
Graphite conducts electricity and also slides very smoothly, so it works as its own lubricant on the copper commutator.
Some brushes mix in metal powder for more current, and tiny motors use thin metal fingers.
Think of a pencil. The "lead" is really graphite, and it writes because thin layers slip off as you slide it.
That same slipperiness makes graphite gentle on the commutator and leaves a thin lubricating film.
The analogy has a limit: unlike a pencil, a brush must also carry current, so its material has to balance conductivity, wear and friction.

With a roughly constant drop per brush, contact loss grows linearly with current ( 2 volts bI ), while the blocks' own ohmic loss ( I to the 2R with R about 5 milliohms) is small by comparison: about 1 watts at 10 amps against 20 watts of contact loss for carbon.
The drops used (1. 0 volts and 0. 3 volts) are typical round numbers for the two families, not data for a specific grade.
Graphite: a form of carbon with slippery layers that conducts electricity. Carbon-graphite brush: the common general-purpose brush material.
Metal-graphite brush: graphite mixed with copper or silver for lower resistance. Commutator: the copper segments the brush slides on.
Contact voltage drop: the voltage lost across the brush contact, roughly 0. 5–1 volts per carbon brush.
Take a carbon brush that drops about 1 volts.
A motor on a 12 volts supply has two brushes in the current path, so it loses about 2 volts, which is 2 / 12, about one sixth of the supply.
For a car starter, that waste matters at very high current, so it uses metal-graphite brushes with a much lower drop.
A tiny toy or camera motor often uses thin precious-metal fingers instead. That is the whole idea: pick the brush material to match the current and size of the motor.
"Most brushes are carbon-graphite.
Graphite is conductive and a natural solid lubricant, so it slides with low friction and leaves a stable film on the copper commutator, and the slightly resistive carbon helps commutation.
Variants: electrographite for better performance, metal-graphite with copper or silver for lower drop and higher current in low-voltage motors, and precious-metal fingers in tiny motors.
It's a trade-off between conductivity, drop, hardness and wear, set by current density and speed."
